title: Linux process model
intro: Questions on how Linux creates, schedules, and terminates processes. Understanding the process model is foundational for scripting, debugging hangs, and writing reliable services.

questions.prompt: What two system calls does a Linux process use to start a new program: one to duplicate itself and one to replace its memory image with a new program?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
`fork()` creates an exact copy of the calling process (same code, data, open files — copy-on-write). `exec()` (family: `execve`, `execvp`, …) replaces the current process image with a new program without creating a new PID.

Shell execution model:
```
bash fork()s → child calls exec(ls) → ls runs as the child
 bash waits for child to exit
```
Servers use fork-without-exec to create worker processes sharing the same code.

questions.prompt: What PID is always assigned to the first user-space process that the Linux kernel starts after booting?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**PID 1** is special:
- It is started directly by the kernel (`/sbin/init` or systemd)
- It cannot be killed with SIGKILL
- When any process becomes orphaned, it is re-parented to PID 1
- On systemd systems, PID 1 also manages the cgroup hierarchy and the journal

`pstree -p` shows the full process tree rooted at PID 1.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a process that has exited but whose parent has not yet called wait() to collect its exit status, leaving a table entry in the process table?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
A **zombie process** (state `Z` in `ps`) has finished executing but its exit status has not been read by its parent. It consumes a process table slot but no CPU or memory.

Zombies are cleaned up when the parent calls `wait()` or `waitpid()`. A large number of zombies indicates a buggy parent. If the parent exits, the zombie is re-parented to PID 1 (systemd), which calls `wait()` automatically.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a process whose parent has terminated, causing the kernel to re-parent it to PID 1?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
An **orphan process** is re-parented to PID 1 (systemd) automatically by the kernel when its parent exits. This is normal and intentional for daemonisation — a process can deliberately double-fork to detach from its parent and become an orphan adopted by init.

Contrast with zombies: orphans are running; zombies have exited but not been waited on.

questions.prompt: What single-character process state code in ps output indicates a process that is runnable — either executing on a CPU or waiting in the run queue?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Process state codes in `ps` output:

| Code | State |
|---|---|
| `R` | Running / runnable |
| `S` | Interruptible sleep (waiting for event) |
| `D` | Uninterruptible sleep (I/O wait) |
| `Z` | Zombie |
| `T` | Stopped (SIGSTOP or debugger) |
| `I` | Idle kernel thread |

A `D` state process cannot be killed — it is blocked in a kernel call waiting for I/O to complete.

questions.prompt: What process state code indicates a process in an uninterruptible sleep — typically blocked waiting for I/O — that cannot be interrupted by signals?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
State `D` (uninterruptible sleep) means the process is inside a kernel code path that must not be interrupted — usually waiting for a disk read, NFS response, or similar. `kill -9` has no effect on a `D` state process.

A sustained `D` state often indicates:
- A hung NFS mount
- A failing disk or driver
- A kernel bug

The only resolution is often a reboot or unmounting the offending resource.

questions.prompt: What is the range of nice values in Linux, from highest scheduling priority (most CPU-favoured) to lowest?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Nice values range from **-20** (highest priority, most CPU-favoured) to **19** (lowest priority). The default is 0. Increasing niceness makes a process more polite to other processes.

```bash
nice -n 10 ./cpu-heavy-script   # start with niceness +10
renice -n 5 -p 1234             # change running process
```
Only root can set negative nice values. The scheduler uses nice to weight CPU time allocation.

questions.prompt: What kernel optimisation allows a parent and child process — immediately after fork() — to share the same physical memory pages until one of them writes to a page?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Copy-on-write (COW)**: after `fork()`, parent and child share the same physical pages, marked read-only. When either process writes to a page, the kernel copies that page so each has its own private copy.

This makes `fork()` very fast — no physical memory is copied upfront. Only pages that are actually modified are duplicated. Programs that fork and exec immediately (shells) never trigger a copy of the parent's data pages.

questions.prompt: In the /proc virtual filesystem, what path contains runtime information — including open file descriptors, memory maps, and environment — for the process with PID 1234?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Each running process has a directory at `/proc/<PID>/` containing:

| File | Content |
|---|---|
| `cmdline` | Null-separated argv |
| `status` | State, UID, memory stats |
| `fd/` | Symlinks to open files |
| `maps` | Memory map |
| `environ` | Environment variables |
| `exe` | Symlink to executable |

```bash
ls -la /proc/1/fd    # open files of PID 1 (systemd)
cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '
```

questions.prompt: What field in /proc/<PID>/status shows the PID of the process that created (is the parent of) the given process?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
```bash
grep PPid /proc/1234/status
# PPid: 1
```
**PPid** (Parent PID) identifies the process that called `fork()` to create this one. Tracing PPid chains up to PID 1 gives the full ancestry.

`ps -o pid,ppid,comm` shows PID, PPID, and command name in a compact table. `pstree` visualises the entire tree.

summaryMarkdown:
## Process states

| Code | State | Killable? |
|---|---|---|
| `R` | Running / runnable | Yes |
| `S` | Interruptible sleep | Yes |
| `D` | Uninterruptible I/O wait | No |
| `Z` | Zombie (exited, not waited) | N/A |
| `T` | Stopped | Yes |
